claims.text: Actively learned moment-tensor potentials can be parameterized using ab initio training data.
The workflow will use a sparse set of high-temperature ab initio configurations.
Active learning will identify configurations exhibiting significant free-energy deviations for addition to the training set.
Targeted perturbative corrections can capture vibrational-entropy contributions.
Targeted perturbative corrections can capture anharmonic effects near melting.
Moment-tensor potentials encode local atomic environments using neighborhood-dependent moment-tensor descriptors.
The moment-tensor descriptors are sensitive to both structural order and anharmonic vibrational effects.
Active learning identifies the most extrapolative configurations from a sparse high-temperature training set.
The proposed potential and perturbative corrections will faithfully reproduce solid and liquid free-energy landscapes near fusion.
The proposed workflow will require far fewer DFT calculations than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
Moment-tensor potentials can attain accuracy near that of their underlying DFT calculations while maintaining a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
The proposed method will predict solid and liquid phase free energies with accuracy nearly matching explicit AIMD.
The proposed method will predict melting temperatures and latent heats with accuracy nearly matching explicit AIMD.
The proposed method will reduce computational time by approximately an order of magnitude relative to AIMD.
The proposed method will achieve faster throughput than TOR-TILD.
The intended initial applicability domain is elemental and binary systems at or above approximately 0.8 times their melting temperature.
Performance in complex multicomponent or extremely anharmonic systems is less certain and may require additional model refinement.
Deviation of more than 5% from AIMD phase-free-energy or melting-observable benchmarks would falsify the hypothesis.
A computational-cost reduction of less than a factor of two relative to TOR-TILD would falsify the hypothesis.
